country.name: Uruguay
country.tagline: An Atlantic-cooled pocket between the River Plate and the ocean, where a Basque pioneer's Tannat became a national identity.

stats.note: INAVI figures reported by La Mañana (Jan 2022): about 6,000 ha in production, roughly 70 million litres of wine a year, about 7 million litres exported. Not in the OIV 2025 top 20; current INAVI totals not verified.

country.overview:
Uruguay is South America's Atlantic wine country. Where Argentina and Chile grow grapes in deserts under the Andes, Uruguay grows them on low, rolling hills a few kilometres from the River Plate estuary and the ocean, at 30 to 35°S, in a humid temperate climate with about 1,000 mm of rain a year spread through every season. The landscape looks more like Bordeaux or the French Basque country than like Mendoza, and that resemblance is the key to its story.

The founding figure is Pascual Harriague, a Basque immigrant from France who planted Tannat near Salto in the north of the country around 1870, using vines brought from Concordia across the Uruguay river. Locals called the grape 'Harriague'. Almost at the same time Francisco Vidiella planted European vines at Colón, near Montevideo, and made the first harvest there in 1883. Italian, Basque and Spanish families built the industry that followed, and by the 1950s Uruguay had about 19,000 ha of vines, many of them hybrids for a thirsty home market.

The modern era began in the late 1980s, when the coming Mercosur trade bloc threatened to flood Uruguay with cheaper Argentine and Brazilian wine. The response, led by INAVI (the national wine institute, created in 1987), was to pull out hybrids, plant clean vinifera stock and bet on quality and on one grape. Tannat, a tough, tannic red from Madiran in south-west France, became Uruguay's signature. Grown in a wetter, more maritime climate and often made with softer extraction, Uruguayan Tannat is rounder and more approachable than Madiran, with dark plum, blackberry and a savoury edge. In 2022 Uruguay had about 1,575 ha of Tannat, about 27% of its vineyard, the largest share of any country.

The industry is small and family-based: more than 1,200 mostly small vineyards and, by INAVI's 2022 figure, about 6,000 ha in production, down from 8,000 ha a quarter-century earlier. Most production is in Canelones and Montevideo, but the most exciting growth is east, in Maldonado's granite hills near Punta del Este, where Bodega Garzón and others make Albariño, Pinot Noir and fresh Tannat, and north, in Rivera's red sands on the Brazilian border. Uruguay declared wine its national drink in 2014. Exports remain modest, mostly to Brazil and the United States, while the home market drinks most of the wine.

history.title: Colonial vines
history.text: Spanish settlers plant vines, probably Moscatel, alongside olives in the Banda Oriental, for table grapes and family wine.

history.title: Los Cerros de San Juan
history.text: Uruguay's oldest commercial winery is founded in Colonia department.

history.title: Harriague plants Tannat in Salto
history.text: Basque immigrant Pascual Harriague plants Tannat cuttings, brought from Concordia in Argentina, near Salto in the north. The grape is known locally as 'Harriague' for decades.

history.title: Vidiella's first harvest at Colón
history.text: Francisco Vidiella harvests his European vines at Colón, near Montevideo, on 25 February 1883, an event remembered as the first national harvest festival. Folle Noire becomes known locally as 'Vidiella'.

history.title: First wine law
history.text: Uruguay's first wine law (17 July 1903) regulates 'natural wine'; quality controls and production census follow in 1904.

history.title: INAVI created
history.text: Law 15.903 creates the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, based in Las Piedras, Canelones; the Vino de Calidad Preferente category follows in 1993, as hybrid vineyards are replaced with vinifera.

history.title: Maldonado's first vines
history.text: Alto de la Ballena plants the first modern vineyard in Maldonado, opening Uruguay's Atlantic frontier.

history.title: Wine becomes the national drink
history.text: Decree 171/014 declares Uruguayan wine, in all its styles, the national drink and requires labels to say so.

history.title: Bodega Garzón
history.text: Alejandro Bulgheroni's Bodega Garzón opens its winery near Pueblo Garzón in Maldonado and is named New World Winery of the Year by Wine Enthusiast in 2018.

country.classification:
Uruguay has no formal denomination of origin system. Wine law, administered by INAVI under laws 15.903 (1987) and 18.462 (2009), divides wine into two main categories: *Vino de Calidad Preferente* (VCP), quality wine from Vitis vinifera, bottled in containers of 75 cl or less, with registered labels; and *Vino Común* (VC), table wine often sold in demijohns or cartons. Under MERCOSUR rules a varietal or vintage claim requires at least 85% of the named grape or year.

Geographic names on labels follow the country's 19 administrative departments (Canelones, Maldonado, Colonia and so on), and producers may use a finer place name if all grapes come from it. The industry and INAVI's promotion group departments into informal regions, commonly six: Metropolitana (Canelones, Montevideo, San José), Oceánica (Maldonado, Rocha, Lavalleja), Litoral Sur (Colonia, Soriano), Litoral Norte (Salto, Paysandú, Artigas), Centro (Durazno, Florida, Tacuarembó) and Norte (Rivera). These groupings have no legal force, and Uruguay notified only the national name for protection in the Mercosur GI agreement. Uruguay was the first South American country to ban foreign place names such as 'Champagne' on domestic labels, in 1993.
country.climate_soils:
Uruguay's climate is humid and temperate, closer to Bordeaux than to Mendoza. Average temperatures are around 17°C, rainfall around 1,000 to 1,100 mm a year spread across all seasons, and sea breezes from the River Plate and the Atlantic cool nights and summer afternoons. That humidity is the great challenge (rot and mildew, vintage variation) and the reason thick-skinned Tannat was the grape that survived best. The south and east are coolest; the northern border departments of Rivera, Salto and Artigas are warmer and more continental.

Geologically, Uruguay is ancient: the Precambrian crystalline shield outcrops as granite and gneiss in the eastern hills of Maldonado and Lavalleja, while the Metropolitan region has heavy, fertile clays and clay-loams, sometimes with calcareous layers. Rivera has deep red sands derived from sandstones, very free-draining, and the western littoral has sedimentary soils shaped by the Uruguay river. INIA's soil inventory identifies dozens of soil types under vine, a lot of diversity for so small an industry.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: The national grape: about 1,575 ha in 2022, roughly 27% of the vineyard. Brought by Pascual Harriague around 1870; softer and rounder than Madiran, often blended with Merlot, Cabernet Franc or Pinot Noir.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: The second red, prized for softening Tannat in blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: Increasingly important for fresh, herbal reds, especially in Maldonado and Canelones.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.note: First planted by Bodega Bouza around 2002; now a signature white of the Atlantic coast and, by INAVI's count, about 128 ha in 2024.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: A leading white, bright and saline in coastal sites.

grapes.name: Marselan
grapes.note: A Cabernet Sauvignon x Grenache cross that has found a second home in Canelones.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Becoming a speciality of Maldonado's cooler, granitic hills and of sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Moscatel (Muscat Hamburg) and Ugni Blanc
grapes.note: Large areas remain for rosé and table wine, though INAVI is encouraging reconversion.

uy-artigas.name: Artigas
uy-artigas.summary: Artigas, the northernmost department, grows grapes around Bella Unión on the Brazilian border, in Uruguay's warmest climate (about 115 ha in 2013).
uy-artigas.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-canelones.name: Canelones
uy-canelones.grapes: Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Marselan, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Albariño, Muscat Hamburg
uy-canelones.terroir: Rolling hills of heavy clay and clay-calcareous soils; humid maritime climate with about 1,000 mm of rain; sea breezes from the River Plate.
uy-canelones.nerd_note: Uruguay grows nearly a third of the world's Tannat, by INAVI and University of Adelaide estimates, and most of it is in Canelones.
uy-canelones.summary: Canelones, immediately north of Montevideo, is Uruguay's wine heartland: by most accounts more than 60% of national production, with Montevideo together over three-quarters of the vineyard. Its gently rolling hills of heavy clay and clay-calcareous soils (around Las Piedras, Progreso, Juanicó, Canelón Chico, Las Violetas and Melilla's edge) are home to the historic family wineries of Italian, Basque and Spanish descent: Pisano, Pizzorno, Carrau, Stagnari, Juanicó, Marichal, Toscanini, De Lucca, Varela Zarranz. Tannat is king, making structured, ageable reds whose tannins are tamed by the maritime humidity, alongside Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Marselan, Sauvignon Blanc and a growing range of Italian and Spanish varieties. INAVI itself is headquartered in Las Piedras.
uy-canelones.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-cerro-largo.name: Cerro Largo
uy-cerro-largo.summary: Cerro Largo, in north-eastern Uruguay on the Brazilian border around Melo, is cattle and rice country with very little commercial viticulture. Its rolling grasslands continue into Brazil's Campanha Gaúcha, where vineyards have spread since the 2000s on similar soils and climate, so it is a plausible future frontier for Tannat.
uy-cerro-largo.terroir: Rolling grassland on sandstone and basalt-derived soils, warmer and more continental than the southern coast.
uy-cerro-largo.nerd_note: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-colonia.name: Colonia
uy-colonia.summary: Colonia, on the River Plate opposite Buenos Aires, has the oldest commercial winery in Uruguay, Los Cerros de San Juan (1854), and a hub of wineries around Carmelo, including Irurtia, Narbona and the Zubizarreta family. The warmer river influence and sedimentary soils make Tannat fuller and riper here.
uy-colonia.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-durazno.name: Durazno
uy-durazno.summary: Durazno, in the centre of the country, has a small, experimental wine scene led by Bodega El Capricho, an early planter of Verdejo and Mencía in Uruguay. Supple reds from warmer inland conditions.
uy-durazno.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-flores.name: Flores
uy-flores.summary: Flores, Uruguay's least populous department, around Trinidad in the centre of the country, has had no registered vineyards since the late 2000s according to official statistics, after earlier small plantings were abandoned.
uy-flores.nerd_note: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-florida.name: Florida
uy-florida.summary: Florida department, north of Canelones, has a few dozen hectares of vines (about 50 ha in 2013).
uy-florida.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-lavalleja.name: Lavalleja
uy-lavalleja.summary: Lavalleja, inland from Maldonado in the eastern sierras, has few vineyards, but Familia Deicas farms an extreme site on the volcanic outcrop of Cerro del Guazuvirá, a rare volcanic terroir in Uruguay.
uy-lavalleja.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-maldonado.name: Maldonado
uy-maldonado.grapes: Albariño, Tannat, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Marselan
uy-maldonado.terroir: Granite, gneiss and decomposed 'balasto' rock on hills up to a few hundred metres; strong Atlantic winds; cooler summers.
uy-maldonado.nerd_note: Garzón's vineyard is split into a large number of small blocks to follow the patchwork of granite and soil depth.
uy-maldonado.summary:
Maldonado is Uruguay's fastest-growing and most glamorous wine region, on granite hills between Punta del Este, José Ignacio and the sierras inland. Nobody planted here until Alto de la Ballena in 2001, because the rocky, poor soils gave low yields; that is exactly what attracted the quality pioneers. The ocean is close, winds are strong and summers fresher, so Tannat comes out brighter and Albariño, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc shine.

Bodega Garzón, built near Pueblo Garzón by Argentine billionaire Alejandro Bulgheroni and opened in 2016, put the department on the world map with hundreds of small vineyard blocks on granite and ballast-like decomposed rock. Viña Edén, Bodega Oceánica José Ignacio, Familia Deicas's Atlántico Sur and Cerro del Toro are among the others.
uy-maldonado.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-montevideo.name: Montevideo
uy-montevideo.summary: Montevideo department holds the historic suburban vineyards of the capital, at Melilla, Colón, Peñarol and Carrasco. Francisco Vidiella made the first harvest of European vines at Colón in 1883, and Bodega Bouza, Carrau's Colón winery, Bodega Santa Rosa and others keep the tradition alive within city limits. Conditions mirror Canelones: clay soils, river-moderated climate, Tannat, Merlot and Albariño.
uy-montevideo.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-paysandu.name: Paysandú
uy-paysandu.summary: Paysandú, on the Uruguay river, has about 170 ha of vines (2013) on sedimentary soils in a warm, continental climate; Tannat and Cabernet ripen fully here.
uy-paysandu.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-rio-negro.name: Río Negro
uy-rio-negro.summary: Río Negro department lies on the Uruguay river around Fray Bentos and Young. Its small vineyards disappeared between roughly 1989 and 2007 according to official vineyard statistics, so today it is a department with a wine past rather than a current scene.
uy-rio-negro.terroir: Alluvial and sedimentary soils near the river, with hot summers.
uy-rio-negro.nerd_note: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-rivera.name: Rivera
uy-rivera.summary: Rivera, on the Brazilian border, is Uruguay's most distinctive northern terroir: deep, red, sandy soils derived from sandstone, very free-draining in a warmer, sunnier climate. The Carrau family pioneered here from the 1970s with the Cerro Chapeu vineyard; the wines, notably Tannat and Cabernet, are fragrant and juicy with silky tannins.
uy-rivera.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-rocha.name: Rocha
uy-rocha.summary: Rocha, the easternmost coastal department towards the Brazilian border, is Uruguay's newest wine frontier, with a handful of small vineyards in windswept coastal and sierra sites.
uy-rocha.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-salto.name: Salto
uy-salto.nerd_note: Uruguayans called Tannat 'Harriague' in the founder's honour for decades.
uy-salto.summary: Salto, on the Uruguay river in the north-west, is where Pascual Harriague planted Tannat around 1870 and where the grape's Uruguayan story began. Today its vineyards are small (about 60 ha in 2013), in a warmer, more continental climate.
uy-salto.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-san-jose.name: San José
uy-san-jose.summary: San José, west of Canelones, is pastoral cattle country with a significant vineyard (about 500 ha in 2013) on the gentle hills around Libertad, Ecilda Paullier and Rincón del Pino. Conditions are similar to Canelones, slightly more influenced by the River Plate.
uy-san-jose.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-soriano.name: Soriano
uy-soriano.summary: Soriano, on the Uruguay river north of Colonia, has a small vineyard area among the grain farms around Dolores and Mercedes.
uy-soriano.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-tacuarembo.name: Tacuarembó
uy-tacuarembo.summary: Tacuarembó, in the north-central interior, has small emerging plantings (about 30 ha in 2013).
uy-tacuarembo.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

uy-treinta-y-tres.name: Treinta y Tres
uy-treinta-y-tres.summary: Treinta y Tres, in the east of Uruguay, takes its name from the 'Thirty-Three Orientals' who launched the 1825 independence campaign. Official statistics record no remaining vineyards here since about 2007, after small plantings faded away.
uy-treinta-y-tres.terroir: Granitic and sandy soils in hilly country.
uy-treinta-y-tres.nerd_note: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

sites.name: Bodega Garzón
sites.text: Opened in 2016 near Pueblo Garzón, about 18 km from the Atlantic, by Argentine energy magnate Alejandro Bulgheroni. A sustainability-certified winery among granite hills, with vineyards split into many small blocks; its Albariño and Tannat made Maldonado famous, and Wine Enthusiast named it New World Winery of the Year in 2018.

sites.name: Pueblo Garzón
sites.text: A near-abandoned railway village that was revived when Argentine chef Francis Mallmann opened his hotel and restaurant in the old general store in 2003. Bodega Garzón's vineyards stretch over the surrounding hills.

sites.name: Alto de la Ballena
sites.text: Planted in 2001 on the Sierra de la Ballena, a granite ridge overlooking the Atlantic near Punta Ballena. The first modern vineyard in Maldonado, it proved that the rocky coastal hills could ripen Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Viognier.

sites.name: Viña Edén
sites.text: An estate in the hills near Pueblo Edén, Maldonado, with a winery set among granite boulders. Known for unoaked, bright Tannat and traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: Bodega Bouza, Melilla
sites.text: The Bouza family's winery in Melilla, on Montevideo's rural edge, in a restored early 20th-century building. Bouza planted Uruguay's first commercial Albariño in the early 2000s and makes single-parcel Tannat (Parcela Única); it also displays a collection of vintage cars and planes.

sites.name: Bodegas Carrau, Colón
sites.text: The Carrau family, winemakers in Catalonia since the 18th century, settled in Uruguay in the 1930s. Their Colón winery in Montevideo makes classic Tannat and pioneered both the Cerro Chapeu vineyard in Rivera and Petit Manseng in Uruguay.

sites.name: Cerro Chapeu, Rivera
sites.text: A vineyard area in Rivera near the Brazilian border, on deep red sandy soils, pioneered by the Carrau family from the 1970s. Its wines, notably Tannat, are fragrant with fine tannins, quite different from the clay-grown Tannat of Canelones.

sites.name: Establecimiento Juanicó
sites.text: A historic estate in Juanicó, Canelones, with an underground cellar built in the colonial era, owned by the Deicas family since 1979. Familia Deicas makes the Preludio blend and extreme-terroir wines from Maldonado and Lavalleja.

sites.name: Pizzorno Family Estates
sites.text: Founded in 1910 by the Italian immigrant Próspero Pizzorno in Canelón Chico, Canelones. Four generations on, the family makes Tannat-based reds and sparkling wines from its estate vineyards.

sites.name: Pisano, Progreso
sites.text: The Pisano family, of Italian origin, farm vineyards around Progreso in Canelones. Brothers Daniel, Eduardo and Gustavo Pisano helped take Uruguayan Tannat to export markets from the 1990s with wines such as the RPF (Reserva Personal de la Familia) range.

sites.name: Los Cerros de San Juan
sites.text: Founded in 1854 in Colonia department, Los Cerros de San Juan is Uruguay's oldest commercial winery. Its estate of stone buildings and old cellars sits by the San Juan river near the River Plate.

sites.name: Carmelo wine route
sites.text: The river port of Carmelo in Colonia is the hub of a small wine route of family wineries (Irurtia, Narbona, El Legado and others) facing the Paraná delta and Buenos Aires across the water.

sites.name: Harriague's Tannat, Salto
sites.text: Near Salto, around 1870, the Basque immigrant Pascual Harriague planted Tannat on an estate north of the city, using cuttings brought from Concordia across the Uruguay river. It was the beginning of Uruguay's national grape.

sites.name: Colón, Vidiella's vineyard
sites.text: At Colón, now a Montevideo suburb, Francisco Vidiella planted European vines and held his first harvest on 25 February 1883, celebrated as Uruguay's first harvest festival. The grape he grew, Folle Noire, became known locally as 'Vidiella'.

sites.name: INAVI, Las Piedras
sites.text: The headquarters of the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, created in 1987, in Las Piedras, the historic wine town of Canelones. INAVI regulates the industry, sets the minimum grape price and runs Uruguay Wine's promotion.
